subject: Retention buckets and field-level sanitization playbook for HIPAA deployments
messages:

Cc: security@healthcorp.com, legal_ops@healthcorp.com
Date: Mon, 3 Nov 2025 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Data retention thresholds + redaction approach for PHI cohorts

Hi Chloe,

Thanks for the demo last week — HealthCorp is excited about Redwood's low-latency options. Before we proceed to a pilot, our security and legal teams have a couple of concrete asks around retention and redaction for PHI-derived data. High level: we need a written approach we can show internally that covers retention limits, how deletions are executed (including backups), and what redaction options you can apply at ingest vs. post-processing.

Specific questions:
- Can you outline recommended retention buckets (short/medium/long) for PII/PHI and whether Redwood supports tenant-scoped retention windows?
- For records that must be "erased" under an access/erasure request (HIPAA right to be forgotten scenarios), how does Redwood guarantee removal from serving caches, KV caches, embeddings stores, and long-term backups?
- What redaction techniques do you support (field-level mask, irreversible hashing, tokenization, full record suppression) and the tradeoffs for downstream model quality?
- How quickly can an erasure be completed end-to-end for a single patient record in the US region, and do you provide time-to-complete SLAs for Dedicated or Private deployments?

We attached a spreadsheet with our expected retention categories and a PDF with a few example records. Can someone from your compliance or security team respond with a short playbook? We need this by EOD Friday to include in our pilot security review.

Best,
Alice
Alice Singer
Security Program Manager — HealthCorp Analytics

Subject: Re: Data retention thresholds + redaction approach for PHI cohorts

Chloe / Marissa / Alice — below is a compact technical playbook we can share with HealthCorp. I'm keeping it pragmatic and highlighting tradeoffs so they understand what we can commit to in Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.

--- Playbook (technical summary) ---
1) Retention Buckets (recommended defaults for PHI)
   - Short (ephemeral): 0-30 days — good for session-only data and transient conversational context. Minimal retention, automatically prunable. Low impact on model quality.
   - Medium (operational): 31-365 days — full records retained for troubleshooting, audit, and retraining sampling. Consider 90/180/365 options depending on customer policy.
   - Long (archival): >365 days — only for explicit business needs; we recommend irreversible redaction/aggregation for PHI if retained.

   Implementation notes: Tenant-scoped retention windows are supported. Per-tenant policies are enforced at the ingestion pipeline and persisted in the metadata layer. Retention sweeps run daily and mark objects for deletion; deletions are then garbage-collected by the storage layer.

2) Deletion guarantees and scope (what we remove)
   - Serving cache / KV cache: entries are TTL'd and can be invalidated immediately for an erasure request. We flag deleted IDs and refuse to serve related KV cache entries; background compaction removes the memory-resident items within minutes to hours depending on load.
   - Embeddings store: we maintain mapping tables from embedding id -> source record. On erasure, we mark the mapping and remove entries from the main vector store. For some vector DBs we support sync-delete; for others we schedule an immediate tombstone + reindex job.
   - Model training data: Hosted Redwood does not retroactively retrain models on customer data by default. If a customer elects to allow training, we can provide processes to exclude erased records from future training runs and maintain logs.
   - Backups / snapshots: backups are an operational constraint. We support two deletion modes: (a) logical deletion — mark record as erased and exclude from serving and future restores; (b) physical purge — delete from primary and attempt to purge from any live snapshot copies. For immutable backups (offsite/archival), we provide documented timelines for purge windows; in Private deployments customers can reduce snapshot retention or manage backups themselves to meet regulatory timelines.

3) Redaction & anonymization primitives
   - Field-level masking: replace sensitive fields (SSN, MRN) with fixed tokens or tokens with deterministic salts. Pros: reversible if salt is kept; low impact on downstream quality if done carefully. Cons: reversible if salt is compromised.
   - Irreversible hashing: cryptographic hash of an identifier (sha256). Pros: non-reversible; good for dedup/checks. Cons: loses original value; model prompts that rely on full fidelity may degrade.
   - Token replacement / canonicalization: replace fields with canonical placeholders (e.g., [PATIENT_NAME], [DOB_YEAR]). Pros: preserves structure for models; low re-identification risk.
   - Field suppression / record suppression: fully remove fields or the whole record. Pros: strongest privacy. Cons: highest impact on model performance and analytics.
   - Pseudonymization service: we support a Vault-backed tokenization service (Private / Dedicated) where tokens map to real values under strict access controls. This provides reversible tokens with audit trail.

   Tradeoffs: embeddings and semantic search are sensitive to redaction strategy. For example, replacing names with [PATIENT_NAME] preserves semantic patterns better than hashing. For PHI fields used as retrieval keys (IDs), deterministic hashing or tokens are preferable. We recommend a hybrid: irreversible hashing for direct identifiers stored in logs/backups; tokenization/pseudonymization for fields used in model context.

4) Timelines / SLAs for erasure (target windows)
   - Hosted API: initial invalidation within 15 minutes; complete KV/serving purge within 24 hours; embeddings and associated vector-store removals within 72 hours (dependent on underlying index). Backups: we commit to excluding erased records from restores starting immediately; complete physical removal from immutable offsite snapshots will follow the backup retention window (we document retention windows during onboarding).
   - Dedicated (reserved capacity): we can commit to accelerated purge SLAs (complete purge within 48 hours) under contract, with operational runbooks and audit logs.
   - Private: customer-controlled backups and configuration allow sub-day physical purges; Redwood provides tooling and a verification checklist.

5) Auditability & proof of deletion
   - We provide deletion audit logs that show tombstone events, GC completion, and vector-store reindex tasks.
   - For enterprise customers we can provide periodic deletion reports and signed attestations for completed erasure workflows.

6) Operational caveats & exceptions
   - Replication lag: cross-region replication may cause short windows where replicas still contain data — we propagate tombstones and reconcile replication within retention windows.
   - Service tickets and support dumps: attachments or support logs that include PHI must be redacted; we recommend customers use tenant-scoped scrubbers before uploading logs to support tickets.

--- end technical summary ---

I'll draft a one-page playbook (PDF) with these bullets and include recommended retention values based on their attached spreadsheet. Chloe/Marissa: I put conservative Hosted timelines above; for Dedicated/Private we should list the contractable SLA options and the verification steps.

Markus
